newsitem.title: USA: COFFEE - U.S. stock drop unlikely to jolt prices.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE - U.S. stock drop unlikely to jolt prices.

text.p: U.S. inventories of green coffee fell last month to their lowest level in seven years, but industry analysts said chances are slim the much-anticipated drawdown will give coffee prices a jolt.
Green coffee stocks housed in U.S. warehouses declined by 93,000 60-kg bags in August, to 1,816,000 bags, their lowest level since May 1989, the Green Coffee Association of New York said on Monday.
Market participants had widely forecast a drawdown of between 50,000 and 200,000 bags.
"This confirms what the market had already discounted," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
"I don't think this number is going to have too much of an impact on tomorrow's market because...people realize that it represents the low for the period," she added.
Inventories will inevitably begin to build over the next one to two months, Ganes said, as coffee currently being harvested in Central and South America makes its way to the U.S.

Coffee futures rallied to four-month highs in late August amid fears of a spot supply shortage, but the market has since retreated sharply as new-crop coffee flows into consumer markets. Indeed, the recent spike in the futures market may have encouraged producers to step up their shipments to the U.S., Ganes said.

Modest gains posted by the arabica futures market in New York on Monday in anticipation of the GCA figures further diminish the chances for a rally when trading resumes tomorrow, said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast.
"This market has almost routinely failed to repsond after the (GCA) number has come out," she said.
"It may wiggle around a bit, but I don't think it will get higher than 106.80 (cents per lb, basis December)," she said.

Many speculators, whose hefty long position was confirmed in the latest Commitment of Traders data released last Friday, may breathe a sigh of relief at the fairly sizable drawdown, said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.
"It may give (the market) a little bit of support, but not a lot," he said. "At least it doesn't give anyone a reason to sell."
Whatever the immediate response to the inventory numbers, the market may benefit in the short-term from an improved technical stance, Platt added.
"The (GCA numbers) are pretty unexciting," he said. "(But) it looks like the market was somewhat overdone. People are a little bit less inclined to be sellers."

While the longer term outlook for coffee continues to point downward, Platt said New York's December contract could test 108 cents, and possibly 110 cents, before heading back toward 100 ($1) per pound.
Prendergast also predicted that coffee futures, already battered by a two-thirds retracement from recent highs, would continue to work its way lower over the next few weeks.
To slow the current fowntrend, December would need to gather enough steam to push through resistance in the 107.90-108.00 cent area, Prendergast said.
